STAT 331/531 Final Project: Basketball Analysis Lab

Author

Elaina Chao, Natalie Murai, Nathan Munoz

Introduction

In this lab, we will analyze Division I college basketball data from the 2013-2026 seasons. The dataset includes team statistics such as wins, losses, offensive efficiency, defensive efficiency, strength of schedule, and tournament-related performance measures.

The goal of this lab is to practice data wrangling, visualization, and functional programming skills using real sports analytics data. This dataset works well for the lab because it contains multiple years of observations, categorical and numeric variables, opportunities for grouping and summarizing, and enough complexity for writing functions and iteration tasks.

Dataset Source

College Basketball Dataset from Kaggle: https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/andrewsundberg/college-basketball-dataset/data

Data Dictionary: Selected Variables

Variable Description
TEAM Team name
CONF Conference
YEAR Season year
G Games played
W Wins
ADJOE Adjusted offensive efficiency
ADJDE Adjusted defensive efficiency
BARTHAG Power rating metric
EFG_O Effective field goal percentage on offense
EFG_D Effective field goal percentage allowed on defense
TOR Turnover rate
WAB Wins above bubble

Learning Goals

This lab is intended to assess the following skills:

  1. Using dplyr verbs for efficient data manipulation.
  2. Creating data visualizations with ggplot2.
  3. Writing functions that take user inputs and return data frame outputs.
  4. Using string and data-cleaning tools to prepare data for analysis.
  5. Interpreting statistical graphics and summaries in context.
  6. Simulation

Setup

library(tidyverse)
library(kableExtra)

basketball <- read_csv("cbb.csv")

Lab Questions

Tip

For questions where you display rows of a data frame, try to only print the rows and columns needed to answer the question.

Question 1: Data Wrangling

Create a new dataset containing only teams from the 2024 season.

Then:

  1. Select the variables TEAM, CONF, W, ADJOE, and ADJDE.
  2. Arrange the teams from most wins to fewest wins.
  3. Display the first 10 rows.

Solution

basketball_2024 <- basketball |>
  filter(YEAR == 2024) |>
  select(TEAM, CONF, W, ADJOE, ADJDE) |>
  arrange(desc(W))

Question 2: Visualization

Using the 2024 season data, create a scatterplot showing the relationship between adjusted offensive efficiency (ADJOE) and adjusted defensive efficiency (ADJDE).

Before making the plot, use fct_collapse() to create a new variable called conference_region that groups conferences into East, Central, and West regions.

Then:

  1. Look at the defined conference regions.
  2. Use fct_collapse() to create conference_region.
  3. Create a scatterplot with ADJOE on the x-axis and ADJDE on the y-axis.
  4. Color the points by conference_region.
  5. Include a title, axis labels, and a legend label.
Note

In this dataset, higher ADJOE values represent stronger offensive efficiency, while lower ADJDE values represent stronger defensive efficiency.

Solution

east_confs <- c("A10", "ACC", "AE", "Amer", "ASun", "BE", "BSth",
                "CAA", "Ivy", "MAAC", "MEAC", "NEC", "Pat", "SC", "SEC")
central_confs <- c("B10", "B12", "CUSA", "Horz", "MAC", "MVC",
  "OVC", "SB", "Slnd", "Sum", "SWAC", "ind")
west_confs <- c("BSky", "BW", "MWC", "P12", "WAC", "WCC")
basketball_2024 <- basketball_2024 |>
  mutate(
    conference_region = fct_collapse(
      .f = CONF,
      "East" = east_confs,
      "Central" = central_confs,
      "West" = west_confs))
basketball_2024 |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ADJOE, y = ADJDE, color = conference_region)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Offensive vs. Defensive Efficiency in the 2024 Season",
    x = "Adjusted Offensive Efficiency",
    y = "Adjusted Defensive Efficiency",
    color = "Conference Region")

Strong teams generally appear with high offensive efficiency and low defensive efficiency. Some conferences may show visible clustering, suggesting similar performance levels among teams in the same conference.

Question 3: Functions: Week 7+ Material

Write a function called top_team() that:

  • takes a conference name as input,
  • filters the dataset to the 2024 season,
  • and returns the team with the highest number of wins in that conference.

Test your function using the "WCC" and "SEC" conferences.

Tip

Your function should return the team, conference, and wins.

Solution

top_team <- function(conf_name) {
  basketball |>
    filter(YEAR == 2024, CONF == conf_name) |>
    arrange(desc(W)) |>
    slice_max(W) |>
    select(TEAM, CONF, W)
}
top_team("WCC")
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  TEAM         CONF      W
  <chr>        <chr> <dbl>
1 Saint Mary's WCC      26
top_team("SEC")
# A tibble: 1 × 3
  TEAM   CONF      W
  <chr>  <chr> <dbl>
1 Auburn SEC      27

Question 4: Data Wrangling

Compare conference performance between the 2013 and 2024 seasons. For each conference, calculate the median adjusted offensive efficiency and median adjusted defensive efficiency in both years.

  • Create one row for each conference.
  • Include columns for 2013 offense, 2024 offense, offense change, 2013 defense, 2024 defense, and defense change.
  • Arrange the table from largest offensive improvement to smallest offensive improvement.
  • Print only the conference name which had the largest offensive improvement.
Tip

This will require transforming your data! Sketch out what you want the final table to look like before you begin coding.

You should be starting with the full basketball dataset and ending with one row per conference.

Tip

Use the median() function to find the typical ADJOE and ADJDE values for each conference in each year.

Offensive/defensive changes can be calculated as: median_offense_2024 - median_offense_2013

Hint: You may need to use ungroup() for your output portion ;)

Solution

conference_table <- basketball |>
  filter(YEAR == 2013 | YEAR == 2024) |>
  group_by(CONF, YEAR) |>
  summarize(
    median_offense = median(ADJOE, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_defense = median(ADJDE, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = YEAR,
    values_from = c(median_offense, median_defense)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    offense_change = median_offense_2024 - median_offense_2013,
    defense_change = median_defense_2024 - median_defense_2013
  ) |>
  drop_na()|>
  arrange(offense_change)

Print only the conference name which had the largest offensive improvement.

conference_table |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_max(offense_change) |>
  pull(CONF)
[1] "SC"

Question 5: Table Cleaning with KableExtra

Using the conference_table you created in Question 4, make a cleanly formatted table that displays the first 8 rows.

Your table should:

  1. Display the top 8 conferences by defensive change.
  2. Add an “Improved Offensively?” column. Indicate: “Significantly” if the offensive change is greater than 5. “Slightly” if the offensive change is less than 5 but greater than 0. “Got Worse” if the offensive change is less than 0.
  3. Use kable_styling() to improve the appearance of the table.
  4. Include a clear title and readable column names.
  5. Clean the values to include only two decimal places.
Tip

You should not need to recreate the table from Question 4. Start with your saved conference_table, then use data manipulation, kable(), and kable_styling() to format the output.

If your table contains NA values, consider adding drop_NA to your data wrangling in question 4.

Solution

conference_table |>
  ungroup() |>
  slice_max(median_offense_2024, n = 8) |>
  mutate(
    offensive_improvement = case_when(
      offense_change >= 5 ~ "Significantly",
      offense_change < 5 & offense_change > 0 ~ "Slightly",
      offense_change < 0 ~ "Got Worse")) |>
 select(
    CONF,
    offense_change,
    offensive_improvement
    ) |>
  kable(
    caption = "Top 8 Conferences by Offensive Improvement from 2013 to 2024",
    col.names = c(
      "Conference",
      "Offense Change",
      "Improved Offensively?"
    ),
    digits = 2
  ) |>
  kable_styling(
    full_width = FALSE,
    bootstrap_options = "striped"
  )

Question 6: Functions: Week 7+ Material

Write a function called win_ratio(). The function should be able to:

  1. Take a data frame, team name, and year as input.
  2. Filter to that team and year.
  3. Calculate the team’s win ratio using wins divided by games played.
  4. Return only that ratio.

##Solution

win_ratio <- function(df, team_name, year) { 
  df |> 
    filter(TEAM == team_name, YEAR == year) |> 
    summarize(win_ratio = W / G) |> 
    pull(win_ratio) 
}

Test your function using the following code chunk:

win_ratio(basketball, "Drake", 2013)
[1] 0.4516129

Question 7: Functions: Week 7+ Material

Write a function called simulate_match(). The function should be able to:

  1. Take a data frame, two team names, and a year as input.
  2. Use win_ratio() to calculate each team’s win ratio for that year.
  3. Use those win ratios to estimate the probability that the first team wins.
  4. Simulate one game between the two teams.
  5. Return the name of the winning team.
Note

For this simulation, we are using a simple Bradley-Terry style model. The probability that Team 1 wins is based on Team 1’s win ratio compared to the total win ratio of both teams.

P(Team 1 Wins) = Team 1 Win Ratio/(Team 1 Win Ratio + Team 2 Win Ratio)

Solution

simulate_match <- function(df, team1, team2, year) { 
  team1_ratio <- win_ratio(df, team1, year)
  team2_ratio <- win_ratio(df, team2, year)
  
  prob_team1 <- team1_ratio / (team1_ratio + team2_ratio)
  
  winner <- sample(
    x = c(team1, team2),
    size = 1,
    prob = c(prob_team1, 1 - prob_team1)
  )
  
  winner
}

Question 8: Simulation: Week 7+ Material

Use map_chr() to simulate 1,000 games between two teams of your choice during the 2024 season.

Then:

  1. Save your results to an object.
  2. Convert the results into a data frame using enframe()
  3. Count how many simulations each team won.
  4. Calculate the proportion of simulations won by each team.
  5. Display your final output using kable()
Tip

Remember to use set.seed() for reproducibility

Solution

set.seed(2005)
results <- map_chr(
  .x = 1:1000,
  .f = ~ simulate_match(
    df = basketball,
    team1 = "Connecticut",
    team2 = "DePaul",
    year = 2024
  )
)

results |>
  enframe(name = "sim", value = "winner") |>
  count(winner) |>
  mutate(prop_won = n / sum(n)) |>
  kable(
    caption = "Simulated Results: Connecticut vs. DePaul",
    col.names = c("Winning Team", "Number of Wins", "Proportion Won")
  )
Simulated Results: Connecticut vs. DePaul
Winning Team Number of Wins Proportion Won
Connecticut 910 0.91
DePaul 90 0.09
